title: Senior's toolkit: building big queries in steps
summary: CTEs you can debug one step at a time, safe recursion, temporary tables for investigations, and editing long queries in the client.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: building big queries in steps
steps.body: Real investigations need queries of 50 lines or more. Seniors build them as named steps, check each step on its own, keep intermediate results in temporary tables, and edit them in a real editor, not on one long prompt line.

toolkit.what: Name each step of a query. To debug, swap the final SELECT for `SELECT * FROM step LIMIT 10` and look at what each step really produces.
flags: later steps can read earlier ones

toolkit.what: Walk trees and graphs: org charts, category trees, bills of materials. Always add a depth limit, because real data has cycles.
flags: the start rows, then how to get the next level
a guard against cycles and runaway data
CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
toolkit.example:
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, manager_id, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 0 FROM staff WHERE id = 7
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.manager_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.id = c.manager_id
  WHERE c.depth < 20
)
SELECT * FROM chain;

toolkit.what: Ask "is there at least one?" per row. It stops at the first match and never multiplies rows, unlike a join.
flags: true if the subquery returns any row
true if it returns none; safe with NULLs
the select list does not matter inside EXISTS
toolkit.example:
SELECT b.id FROM builds b
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM downloads d WHERE d.build_id = b.id AND d.ip NOT LIKE '10.%');

toolkit.cmd: CREATE TEMP TABLE suspects AS SELECT ...
toolkit.what: Save an intermediate result for the rest of your session. Later queries are fast and stable while you investigate, and the table disappears when you disconnect.
flags: visible only to your connection, dropped at the end of the session
create and fill it in one statement

toolkit.what: Tell the planner whether to compute a CTE once or fold it into the main query (PostgreSQL 12+, SQLite 3.35+). Use it when a plan shows the CTE is run the wrong way.
flags: compute once and reuse, like a temporary result
inline it so filters can be pushed into it

toolkit.what: Edit and run long queries from files instead of the prompt line.
flags: psql: open the last query in $EDITOR, run it when you save and quit

steps.prompt: A recursive CTE that walks the reporting chain ran for ten minutes and was killed. It worked fine last month. What is the most likely cause?
code: SELECT id, manager_id FROM staff WHERE id = 7
SELECT s.id, s.manager_id FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.id = c.manager_id
options: Someone created a cycle (A manages B, B manages A), so the recursion never ends; add a depth column with `WHERE depth < 20` or use `CYCLE` in PostgreSQL
The staff table grew past the recursion limit of SQL
Recursive CTEs need an index on `manager_id` to finish
steps.explain: A recursive CTE stops only when a step returns no new rows. On a cycle that never happens. A depth guard costs nothing on good data and turns a hang into a result you can inspect.

steps.prompt: Complete the reporting-chain query with a cycle guard.
code: SELECT id, manager_id, 0 FROM staff WHERE id = 7
FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.id = c.manager_id
steps.explain: `WITH RECURSIVE` lets the CTE refer to itself. The anchor and the recursive step are combined with `UNION ALL` (or `UNION`, which also removes duplicate rows).

steps.prompt: Arrange the query so each step reads only steps defined before it.
lines: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payments GROUP BY customer_id
SELECT customer_id FROM paid WHERE total > 1000
SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN big b ON b.customer_id = c.id;

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the situation.
pairs: a 60-line query you want to read and debug in parts
keep a list of suspect users for the next hour of questions
builds that were downloaded at least once from outside
the plan re-runs an expensive CTE for every reference
fix line 40 of the query you just ran in psql

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Write long queries as named steps and run each step on its own before trusting the whole. Keep investigation queries in a `.sql` file you run with `\i` or `.read`, so you can repeat them tomorrow and paste them into the incident notes.
